title: Pentagon Faces Funding Crisis as Iran War Costs Spiral Beyond $29 Billion
excerpt: The Defense Department is burning through cash faster than expected, but key Republicans are balking at a $95 billion emergency spending package, demanding more transparency on war costs and strategy before signing off.
body:
• The Pentagon has spent at least $29 billion on the Iran war since February, but analysts estimate actual costs could exceed $100 billion when base damage and aircraft losses are included.
  • House Republicans have advanced a $95 billion emergency spending framework, allocating up to $73 billion for defense, but internal GOP divisions threaten its passage.
  • Pentagon officials warn they could run out of operational funding by mid-August, with 45-61% of Patriot missile stockpiles and up to 80% of THAAD interceptors already expended.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune and several Republican lawmakers have expressed skepticism, demanding detailed cost breakdowns and a clear exit strategy before approving new funds.

Four months into Operation Epic Fury, the Pentagon is running out of money — and the political will to replenish it is far from guaranteed.

In a closed-door briefing earlier this month, senior defense officials sat down with House spending leaders from both parties to plead for emergency cash. According to CNN, when pressed for specifics, Pentagon officials were unable to explain why they need the money so urgently, frustrating lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

A $95 Billion Gamble

House Speaker Mike Johnson last week unveiled a $95 billion emergency spending plan that would direct up to $73 billion to the Pentagon and intelligence agencies, $12 billion toward agricultural aid, and $10 billion for state election grants tied to President Trump's SAVE America Act.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Dq5aiE6LAi4

The House Budget Committee advanced the framework on Thursday, but its passage through the full chamber — let alone the Senate — remains uncertain. House Republicans hold a razor-thin 219-212 majority, meaning they can afford only a handful of defections.

"Is the juice worth the squeeze?"

— John Thune, Senate Majority Leader

Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio called the bill "DOA," while Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania declined an invitation to Camp David, calling it a "sales pitch" and demanding a detailed walkthrough of the spending. One unnamed Republican lawmaker who attended a four-hour Pentagon briefing told CNN the defense officials failed to make a compelling case: "The microphones didn't even work. They are asking for $1.5 trillion and they had chips and dip."

The True Cost of War

The Pentagon's acting comptroller, Jay Hurst, testified before Congress in May that the Iran war had cost $29 billion. He has not provided an updated figure since, and that estimate does not include damage to U.S. military installations or the destruction of at least 42 American aircraft, according to a Congressional Research Service report.

https://x.com/agtprpnabsrdty/status/2079318917294547104

Independent analysts and U.S. officials estimate the actual financial toll could reach $100 billion when factoring in extensive base damage — particularly to the Navy's Fifth Fleet headquarters in Manama, Bahrain, and installations in Kuwait — as well as depleted missile stockpiles, according to NBC reporting.

The munitions situation is dire. A Center for Strategic and International Studies report from April estimated the U.S. has used between 45% and 61% of its Patriot missile stockpile, and between 52% and 80% of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors. Manufacturers cannot replenish them fast enough.

"Many bottlenecks exist, including shortages of key critical minerals, motors, and advanced electronics," Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow at Defense Priorities, told the Daily Caller. "Money is not a quick fix."

Mounting Casualties, Mounting Pressure

The funding battle coincides with a spike in American casualties. At least 17 U.S. service members have been killed since the war began on February 28, with the most recent deaths occurring at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 18. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed nearly 100 service members were injured in Iranian attacks since July 7 alone, though he said 96% sustained minor injuries and returned to duty.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine are scheduled to appear before the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday to defend the White House's supplemental funding request, which in its original June submission sought $67 billion for the Pentagon. That request itemized $21 billion for munitions, $17.3 billion for operational costs, $12.1 billion for classified programs, and $5.1 billion for cybersecurity, among other line items.

Implications for the Indian Diaspora

The conflict's escalation has direct consequences for the Indian diaspora and India's strategic calculations. Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — a waterway carrying roughly one-fifth of global oil supply before the war — have pushed energy prices higher, hitting India's import bill hard. The Indian government, which has maintained a cautious diplomatic stance, is also watching the conflict's impact on its citizens working in Gulf states including Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain, all of which have seen U.S. bases targeted by Iranian strikes.

What Comes Next

Speaker Johnson aims to bring the budget framework to a House floor vote before the August recess. But Senate leaders have signaled they want more defense money than the House plan provides, and incoming Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson — a fiscal hawk — may push for spending offsets that could doom the bill in the House.

Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa captured the frustration shared by many in Congress. "Our number-one job as a nation is to provide for national defense," she said. "They need to come to Congress and explain exactly what is going on, what they're going to achieve with those dollars, and really how we wrap this conflict up."

With the Pentagon warning that money for operations could dry up by mid-August, the clock is ticking — and neither party seems ready to write a blank check.
